title: Different types of COVID-19 misinformation have different emotional valence on Twitter
screen_reason: The paper's aim is sentiment analysis, but it devotes a results subsection ('How much misinformation do we observe?') to the share of COVID-19 tweets that are misinformation and reports it with an explicit denominator: about 100,000 of the nearly 17.5 million hashtag-collected tweets were related to fact-checked debunked stories. That is a CONTENT share. A second, narrower share (29% of the manually assessed candidate tweets) is also reported.

estimates.measure_type: % of English COVID-19 hashtag tweets that relate to a fact-checked, debunked COVID-19 story
estimates.value_raw: about 100,000 of the nearly 17.5 million tweets were related to misinformation that we captured (100,000/17,463,220)
estimates.denominator: 17,463,220 English-language, retweet-excluded tweets collected in March 2020 through 76 COVID-19 hashtags (from Chen et al.'s public 123-million-tweet coronavirus dataset)
estimates.definition: The tweet matched one of 226 keyword classifiers built from COVID-19 stories debunked by fact-checking organisations and indexed in Google Fact Check Explorer (all ratings, e.g. misleading or false), and was manually confirmed to be about that debunked story.
estimates.misinfo_def: false, inaccurate, or misleading information designed, presented and promoted to intentionally cause public harm or for profit
estimates.source_quote: about 100,000 of the nearly 17.5 million tweets were related to misinformation that we captured.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'How much misinformation do we observe?', p. 7
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Falsity comes from fact-checking organisations' debunks indexed in Google Fact Check Explorer (226 unique English COVID-19 stories, March 2020, all ratings kept). Two annotators independently extracted the first keyword for each story (identical for 89% of stories, disagreements resolved by discussion); story typology coded by two raters, Krippendorff alpha = 0.74. Whether a matched tweet actually referred to the debunked story was then checked by hand on a random 100 tweets per story; no reliability statistic is reported for that tweet-level check.
estimates.moderator_quote: Our initial sample of tweets was obtained through a public coronavirus Twitter dataset containing over 123 million tweets, with over 60% of them in English collected through 76 hashtags related to COVID-19 (Chen et al., 2020).
estimates.notes: The percentage is not printed; both counts are, so 100,000/17,463,220 = 0.57%. Treat as a soft ceiling-and-floor rather than a measurement: the numerator is the authors' own 'roughly extrapolating' estimate from the manual check of the keyword-matched pool, and 29% of 690,004 would be about 200,000, so the stated 100,000 is not reproducible from the numbers given in the text. It is also a floor in one respect (only misinformation that fact-checkers had already debunked in the same month could be captured) and a ceiling in another (a tweet counts if it discusses the debunked claim, including tweets debunking or mocking it - the paper does not separate endorsement from discussion). Country not stated; English-language only, coded Global. Kept because the Discussion reports it as a headline ('Within the tweets we analyzed, we found ~29% are related to misinformation') and it is the input to the 100,000 extrapolation in the row above. missed_or_uncertain: 1) NOT extracted: 'The average was 9.3 +/- 16.6 related tweets (range: 0-89)' out of 100 analysed per story. This is a mean count per story, not a share of a defined denominator, and it does not agree with the 29% figure (which counts duplicate copies), so I left it out; an adjudicator may prefer it as the more conservative per-story hit rate. 2) NOT extracted: the raw keyword-match rate 690,004 / 17,463,220 = 3.95%. The authors are explicit that most of those matches are false positives (only ~29% were confirmed related), so this is a classifier yield, not a prevalence, and reporting it would overstate misinformation by roughly sevenfold. 3) NOT extracted: 2,097 / 17,463,220. The 2,097 come from a 100-per-story sample, not from the whole corpus, so that ratio has no meaning. 4) NOT extracted: the sentiment splits (86.15% neutral, 6.85% positive, 6.99% negative) and per-type compound scores - these are emotional valence within misinformation tweets, not veracity. 5) NOT extracted: the story-type distribution in Table 1 (cures 18.6%, politics 23.5%, virus 19.0%, conspiracy 14.6%, vaccine 9.7%, other 14.6%) - shares of the 226 debunked stories by topic, i.e. a composition of an all-false set with no non-misinformation denominator. 6) NOT extracted: Kouzy et al.'s '~25% of the analyzed tweets include misinformation' and Brennen et al., cited from elsewhere (R8). 7) Judgement call for an adjudicator: the numerator counts tweets that 'discuss' or 'relate to' a debunked claim, which includes debunking and mocking tweets; the paper does not code stance. If the review requires the numerator to be endorsement or propagation of the false claim, this estimate is an overcount of an already very small number.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of platform data. Corpus: 17,463,220 English-language, retweet-free tweets from March 2020, drawn from Chen et al.'s public coronavirus collection of over 123 million tweets gathered through 76 COVID-19 hashtags. Misinformation ground truth: 226 unique English COVID-19 stories debunked by fact-checking organisations and indexed in Google Fact Check Explorer with a claim or review date between 1 and 31 March 2020, all ratings kept; 247 before de-duplication. Each story was turned into a two-stage keyword classifier by two independent annotators (identical first keyword for 89% of stories; disagreements settled by discussion). Story typology coded by two raters, Krippendorff alpha = 0.74. Keyword matching returned 690,004 tweets, of which a random 100 per story (or all, where fewer) were manually screened for genuine relatedness; unrelated and duplicate tweets removed, leaving 2,097. Only 195 of 226 stories had any matched tweet. No reliability statistic for the tweet-level relatedness screening; no stance coding, so tweets debunking a false claim are counted alongside tweets asserting it. Sampling frame is hashtag-based, so it excludes COVID-19 tweets without one of the 76 hashtags. Not applicable: response rate.
rob.item6_quote: Thus, we apply a general definition of misinformation and disinformation inspired by Buning et al. (2018) "false, inaccurate, or misleading information designed, presented and promoted to intentionally cause public harm or for profit."
rob.item10_quote: The selection based on keywords yielded 690,004 tweets, out of 17,463,220 tweets. [...] The selected tweets together with copies (that were excluded for further analysis) made up 29% of the manually assessed tweets, and roughly extrapolating would mean that about 100,000 of the nearly 17.5 million tweets were related to misinformation that we captured.
